newsitem.title: UK: British, Irish leaders to meet on N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: British, Irish leaders to meet on N.Ireland.

text.p: The British and Irish Prime Ministers will meet in London on December 9 to discuss the troubled Northern Ireland peace process amid fears of a new outbreak of violence by IRA guerrillas.

Prime Ministers John Bruton of Ireland and John Major of Britain will review peace talks under way in Belfast as the Irish leader tours European Union capitals to discuss the EU summit it is holding on December 13 and 14.

Bruton's trip was announced 24 hours after Major effectively rejected proposals by the IRA guerrillas' political wing, Sinn Fein, aimed at getting Sinn Fein invited to the peace talks and restoring a broken 17-month IRA truce.

Britain and Ireland refuse direct talks with Sinn Fein because of the guerrillas' return to war in February this year and the party's proposals were conveyed to the two governments by Irish nationalist politician John Hume.
The IRA renewed its war against British rule in Northern Ireland last February but has not carried out any attacks for nearly two months.
Major said on Tuesday that Britain was not prepared to alter its policy on Northern Ireland which says the IRA must call a credible truce to get Sinn Fein invited to the peace talks.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said he did not believe Major's response was a final or completely negative one. Negotiations for a new ceasefire would continue, he said.
"We are going to continue with our efforts to bridge the gap that exists. The prize is worth taking risks for, and I believe everybody interested in the process will do so," Spring said.

Under the Hume-Sinn Fein proposals, Sinn Fein would be admitted to the talks chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell as soon as the IRA renewed its ceasefire. Demands that the guerrillas disarm immediately would be dropped and a strict timetable would be set for the talks.
They also called for goodwill proposals from Britain, such as the release of some IRA prisoners.
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said Major's rejection of the plan meant the IRA would not call a new truce, raising fears in Northern Ireland of new guerrilla attacks.

Major's rejection early this year of a proposal by Mitchell that the disposal of arms should be addressed during the talks provoked the IRA into abandoning its ceasefire and setting off the first of a series of attacks on British targets.
The republicans' rivals, pro-British "Loyalists", have been allowed into the peace talks because their guerrillas are still honouring a ceasefire originally called to match the IRA's.
Hume has accused Major of rejecting his plan for a new IRA truce to satisfy unionist politicians in the British parliament on whom Major relies to shore up his majority of just one.
Unionists, who can usually be relied on to vote with the government, have threatened to withdraw their support if Major makes any concessions to the republicans, their sworn foes.

Unionists are supported by the 60 percent Protestant majority in Northern Ireland which wants the province to stay British and opposes Irish nationalists who seek its reunification with the Irish republic.
